newsitem.title: USA: Rover Sojourner to begin exploring surface of Mars.
newsitem.headline: Rover Sojourner to begin exploring surface of Mars.

text.p: The Mars rover rolled down a ramp from the Pathfinder space lander late on Saturday onto the surface of the "Red Planet", leaving a clear tire mark in the planet's dust.
"Six wheels on the ground," reported flight director Chris Salvo as the signal came in that the rover was on the ground.
The six-wheeled buggy-type vehicle named "Sojourner" was scheduled to begin exploring the surface of Mars on Sunday, analysing its rocks and soil for at least one week.
Whoops of joy and cheers erupted in the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's mission control here when the signal came through confirming the rover had made it to the Martian surface.

"Rover remember to call home occasionally," said the announcer for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's television as an image appeared of the buggy at the foot of the ramp with a distinct tire mark leading back to the ramp of the landing vehicle.

The successful deployment came after a day of suspense at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, where space officials had feared the scientific aspects of the $266-million mission might be hurt by a communications glitch.
However, communications between the lander and Sojourner were later restored, allowing signals from mission control to get through to the rover's on-board computer.

After a ramp was lowered, the rover was told to "stand-up" from its stowed position. Once the wheels were locked in place, the tiny 22-pound (10 kg) vehicle -- looking like a workbench or microwave oven on wheels -- slowly moved down the 35-degree slope.
At 10:46 p.m. PDT (0546 GMT) the announcer said Sojourner was half-way down the ramp. Then at 10.59 p.m. PDT (0559 GMT Sunday) the rover was confirmed to be on the planet's surface.

During its exploration, the solar-powered rover will navigate with the aid of laser beams, will take 3-D photographs with its twin-lens camera and will be able to pick up and analyse samples of rocks and soil and transmit the data to Earth.
